Warm water in labour: showers, birth pools and safety

Updated: November 14, 2026

Written and edited by BeMama Authors team: checked against published guidance from recognized health organizations.

An old film may show a midwife asking someone to boil water and bring towels. For someone planning a birth today, there are three different questions behind that scene. What keeps equipment clean? Can warm water help with contractions? And what changes if the baby is actually born under water? Each has a different answer, and you can use a pool for part of labour without committing to giving birth in it.

Why the kettle and towels appear in birth stories

In a home without running hot water, heating a pot made warm water available for washing. Towels and dry linen could be useful before and after the birth. A scene in a film cannot tell us why a particular midwife asked for them, or establish that the same practice prevailed everywhere. What people needed for washing is also a different question from what makes an instrument safe to use.

Today, maternity services use clean hands, clean surfaces and appropriate single-use or properly processed equipment. An instrument that enters sterile tissue requires a validated sterilisation process. Boiling something on a stove cannot verify that it has been sterilised. A birth partner can help by finding the clean towels the midwife requests or making room for the team to work. There is no need to carry a pan of boiling water near the bed, pool or baby.

Warmth while contractions build

A comfortably warm shower may help you relax between contractions. Some people enjoy water directed toward the lower back, while others prefer to keep moving on dry land. The point is how you feel. A hot bath has not been shown to start labour reliably. If you have been asked to attend for monitoring or induction, a bath is no reason to postpone that assessment.

Shivering, weakness or feeling faint deserves attention, especially with bleeding or feeling unwell. Ask the maternity team to assess you before going into a bath, and tell them if the sensation starts while you are in the water. The hottest temperature you can tolerate is an unsafe guide. For a wash after birth, wait until you feel steady and ask for assistance if needed. A dry towel, a change of clothing or a warm blanket may be more useful at that moment.

Using a pool during the first stage

During the first stage of labour the cervix opens. A pool lets some people kneel, lean forward or change position more comfortably while the midwife checks them and the baby. Immersion can help with pain, and some people who use it have less need for additional pain relief. A pool cannot promise a shorter labour or predict whether you will need an epidural or an assisted birth.

When you discuss the plan, ask how staff will check the baby’s heart rate in the water, how you will get in and out and what other pain relief is available. You can ask to leave at any time. Your partner can keep the way out clear, stay within calling distance and let the midwife know if you feel too warm, dizzy or uncomfortable. You can also choose to have a shower without using a pool.

The decision can change during labour

Most research on water birth involves healthy people with uncomplicated pregnancies at term and an expected vaginal birth. A safe exit from the pool matters as much as being able to get in. Facilities differ in their equipment, staffing and ability to monitor in water. A figure on a scale alone, such as a fixed body-weight limit from another facility, cannot determine your own options.

Ask ahead if a condition such as epilepsy, high blood pressure or diabetes affects your monitoring or the support you would need. Tell the unit promptly about bleeding, fever, reduced fetal movements, fluid that is green or brown, or possible labour before 37 weeks. Contact them when your waters break according to your maternity plan. The assessment may change what is appropriate even if you previously planned a water birth. NICE advises waiting at least two hours after an opioid given for labour pain before entering a bath or pool. If you still feel drowsy, stay out and tell your midwife.

Comfortable water and clean equipment

The midwife checks both your temperature and the water temperature. For example, UK NICE guidance calls for hourly checks during labour in water and sets 37.5°C as an upper limit for the water. That is a limit for a monitored pool, not a temperature to aim for at home. Tell the midwife if you feel uncomfortable between checks. Avoid adding hot water near anyone in the pool.

Ask how staff prepare, clean and fill the pool and how they would help you out quickly. Ordinary tap water is not sterile. Water that stands warm for a long time can support bacterial growth, and a jetted spa is different from a birth pool maintained under an infection-control protocol. A family should not have to devise cleaning procedures or decide whether equipment can be safely reused.

What changes if the baby is born in water

During the second stage the baby moves through the birth canal and is born. The maternity team needs to be able to assess the baby promptly, manage a cord problem or bleeding and help you move if urgent care is needed. You may decide to leave for the birth even if you found the pool helpful during contractions. Agree in advance how the team will explain a change of plan and where they would help you give birth.

Professional guidance differs. NICE updated its guidance in 2025 to support considering water birth after a discussion of benefits and risks. The American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists reaffirmed its 2016 guidance in April 2025. It supports immersion in the first stage for selected healthy pregnancies and advises giving birth on land. Ask which guidance the unit follows, which patients its service can support and which options are available if a pool is occupied or you need different care.

What the outcome studies can tell you

A large UK study followed people who used a labour pool and compared selected births in water with births after leaving the pool. In low-risk settings, the findings were reassuring for the outcomes studied. The choice to stay in the pool was not assigned at random. People who develop concerns may leave for additional care, so a difference between groups does not automatically describe what would happen to one person choosing either option.

NICE’s evidence review found possible reductions in severe tears for those who had given birth before, heavy bleeding after birth and neonatal unit admission. It also found a higher chance of the umbilical cord snapping before it was clamped. The evidence could not establish a difference in the chance of the baby dying. These distinctions are more useful than a blanket promise of fewer cuts, no tears or a faster delivery. Ask which outcomes are known for people with your obstetric history.

Keeping the baby warm and recognising illness

After birth, the team checks breathing and temperature and dries the baby. Skin-to-skin contact with a warm covering can support a stable newborn while the parent and baby are observed. A baby who needs help breathing needs prompt assessment and care. Routine washing can wait. WHO advises delaying the first bath for at least 24 hours. There is no need to wash away every trace of the creamy protective coating on a newborn’s skin.

Rare serious infections have been reported after water birth, including pneumonia from Legionella bacteria. Case reports identify a possible hazard but cannot tell you how common it is in a well-managed service. If your newborn is breathing unusually fast or with effort, is difficult to wake for feeds, feeds poorly or has an abnormal temperature, seek urgent medical help and tell the team about the water birth. Severe breathing difficulty, blue lips or unresponsiveness needs emergency help.

Evidence-informed guidance

What trusted health organizations recommend

Consider labour immersion and delivery under water as separate choices.

Discuss local protocols, eligibility, temperature checks, monitoring, safe exit and how the service handles an urgent change.

Interpret comparisons of selected low-risk births alongside their observational design and the uncertainty around rare outcomes.

How BeMama can help

BeMama explains how birth-pool decisions are made. Your maternity team can advise on your pregnancy, the birth setting and signs that need assessment.

When to seek help

Contact maternity services promptly for bleeding, fever, reduced fetal movements, coloured amniotic fluid or suspected preterm labour. After birth, urgent help is needed for heavy bleeding or an unwell newborn. Severe breathing difficulty, blue lips, collapse or unresponsiveness requires emergency care.

Evidence notes updated: November 14, 2026

Key takeaways

  • Clean linen, sterile instruments and comfortable warm water each serve a different purpose.
  • You can use a shower or pool for comfort and still choose to give birth on land.
  • Ask about temperature checks, fetal monitoring, pain relief and help getting out of the pool.
  • Evidence on water birth applies mainly to selected uncomplicated pregnancies at term.
  • A newborn’s immediate needs include checking breathing, drying and keeping warm. The first bath can wait.

Frequently asked questions

Why did birth attendants ask for boiling water?

Heating water made warm water available where it was needed for washing. Practices varied, and a historical story is not an instrument-processing standard. Today, maternity teams use appropriate sterile instruments and infection-control procedures.

What about the blood, wet sheets and towels?

Birth involves normal body fluids. The team can replace wet linen, clean surfaces and handle used materials according to its infection-control procedures. Clean dry towels also help keep a stable newborn warm. No one needs to wash a parent or baby with very hot water.

Does a person in labour need hot water if they feel cold?

A warm covering or a comfortable wash may feel good. Let the midwife know about shaking, fever, weakness or light-headedness so the cause can be assessed. Hot water can burn skin and cannot treat an infection or dangerous bleeding.

What are the risks of a water birth?

A cord can snap before clamping, and rare serious newborn infections have been reported. Staff also need to recognise bleeding, breathing problems or difficulty maintaining temperature and provide care promptly. Which benefits and risks apply depends on your pregnancy and the service’s equipment and experience.

Can a hot bath bring on labour?

A warm bath or shower may ease discomfort. There is no good evidence that increasing the heat starts labour, and getting overheated can make you feel unwell. Contact maternity services for advice on symptoms or an agreed induction plan.

Can I use the pool and later ask for an epidural?

Yes, you can change your preference. Tell your midwife when you are considering an epidural so they can discuss getting out, the time needed and whether transfer to another area is necessary. Availability and monitoring arrangements vary.

Should a baby born in water have a bath immediately?

Routine bathing can be delayed. Drying, checking breathing and keeping the baby warm come first. WHO recommends waiting at least 24 hours for the first bath; the team will explain any clinical reason for different care.

This article is general education, not medical advice, diagnosis, or treatment. Always talk with a qualified healthcare professional about your situation, and seek urgent care for emergencies.
